description: We’re NEU Cosmos, a Seattle team building a browser game for young astronauts. Players will run a lunar outpost and decide how to share limited power between life support, communications, and science. Each choice changes what the crew can do next. We’d love to team up with people interested in game design, web development, UI/UX, or science education.
summary:
Groundline turns NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar into a sinking-ground map anyone can open in a browser. Pumping groundwater makes land subside. In California's San Joaquin Valley it has cost one canal more than 60% of its capacity along a stretch, and the State's official subsidence map comes out months late.

We built an open pipeline that reads every NISAR L2 GUNW interferogram over a place, stacks the 12-day pairs into a displacement time series, ties it to GPS, and publishes it as an interactive map with a timeline, 3D view, infrastructure profiles and CSV/GeoJSON download. Pipeline v2 reads only the needed chunks of the HDF5 science products, removes the ionosphere, gives every cell an uncertainty, and passes each site through a quality gate frozen before testing.

Results: at GPS station P307 (Madera), GPS reads -5.8 cm and our map -5.9 cm; Mexico City matches GPS within about 1 cm all year. We found that crops make the radar read about 4 cm too deep (32 of 32 towns), so farmland is flagged and left out of every count. Our confirmed floor: at least 170,900 people live on ground that sank 5 cm or more. The same engine has measured 17 places outside existing free subsidence services.
details:
What it does

Groundline is a free web map of where the ground is sinking, built from NISAR, the new NASA-ISRO L-band radar satellite. It opens on California's San Joaquin Valley, where groundwater pumping has made the land sink so much that canals lose capacity (one stretch of the Friant-Kern Canal lost more than 60%, and repairing ten miles cost about $326 million). The official State map arrives months late; NISAR revisits every 12 days.

The app lets anyone search a place, play a timeline of ground change from November 2025 to October 2026, switch between a map and a 3D view, click any spot or GPS station for its time series, see profiles along the Friant-Kern Canal, California Aqueduct, Delta-Mendota Canal, State Routes 99/43/198, Interstate 5 and the high-speed rail alignment, share a link to the exact view, and download the data as CSV or GeoJSON. A guided six-step tour tells the story. A world view shows which places are checked against GPS, which are measured but not yet checked, and which are still waiting.

How it works

1. Find: query the Alaska Satellite Facility search API for every NISAR L2 GUNW interferogram on one track and frame over the place.

2. Read: pipeline v2 reads only the 512x512 HDF5 chunks over the site with HTTPS byte ranges (about 35-40 MB per pair instead of 2.3 GB): unwrapped phase, coherence, connected components, ionosphere phase screen and the product mask. (Pipeline v1 decoded the public preview PNGs back into phase by inverting the twilight colour map exactly, so it needs no login.)

3. Stack: subtract the ionosphere screen, keep coherent cells in the main connected component, fit a robust plane plus a phase-elevation term from the Copernicus GLO-90 DEM, reference to a stable area, and sum the chain of consecutive 12-day pairs.

4. Uncertainty: every cell and date gets a 1-sigma uncertainty from epoch noise, coherence-based decorrelation and gap filling.

5. Quality gate: seven checks (pairs, usable land, surviving cells, noise, reference coherence, signal above noise) frozen on 14 Nov 2026 after calibrating on two sites and before any other site was run. A site that fails is not published.

6. Check: compare with daily GPS from the Nevada Geodetic Laboratory, with California's official InSAR map (DWR / TRE ALTAMIRA) and with NASA OPERA DISP-S1.

What we found

- It works where it can be checked. At GPS station P307 in Madera, GPS reads -5.8 cm and the map around it -5.9 cm. Over towns and open land in the State's sinking areas, our map (-4.1 cm) matches the State map (-4.15 cm). In Mexico City the map tracks GPS station MMX1 with an RMS of 0.7 cm (r = 0.997).

- Crops fool the radar. Fields read about 4.1 cm lower than the town they surround, in 32 of 32 towns, and the extra signal follows the crop calendar. Rather than hide this, we flag farmland (USDA Cropland Data Layer) as "reads too deep, not counted" and leave it out of every number. Our people count dropped from 400,900 to a confirmed floor of at least 170,900 people on ground that sank 5 cm or more.

- It runs elsewhere. We ran the frozen gate on 27 gap regions outside existing free services (OPERA, EGMS). 13 now have a published map; 12 that passed the gate but whose sinking bowl did not match the literature are shown as "unconfirmed", with no number of ours.

Benefits and intended impact

Water agencies, canal operators, city planners and residents can see within weeks, not months, where the ground is moving, and decide where to send survey crews. Because NISAR is global and free, the same engine can give a first map to places such as Iran, Turkey, Mexico or South Asia that have no national subsidence service. We designed it to be trusted: every number says whether it has been checked, and the limits are on the page.

Tools and languages

Python (numpy, scipy, scikit-image, h5py, rasterio, requests, pillow) for the pipeline; plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with Leaflet and three.js for the app, with no server and no build step. It is hosted on GitHub Pages and also works offline from disk. Node.js scripts check data integrity and run the page logic as a smoke test. GitHub Actions deploys the site. SI coding assistant: Claude (Anthropic).

What makes it creative

We turned public preview images into measurements by inverting their colour map. We stream only the bytes we need from multi-gigabyte science products. And instead of reporting the biggest number, we built the map to refuse what it cannot confirm: a frozen quality gate, per-cell uncertainty, a cropland filter, and an "unconfirmed" status for sites whose signal does not match the literature.

What we considered

Honesty over impact: the cropland effect cut our headline number by more than half, and we published the lower one. Accessibility: the page works on phones, offline, honours reduced motion, and every icon has a tooltip. Colour: one shared ramp (amber to crimson for sinking, teal for rising) used by the map, charts and 3D view. Limits we state on the page: the radar measures along its line of sight, not true vertical; the cause of the crop effect is not identified; the record is short (many regions start mid-2026); and it is not for engineering design or enforcement.
